title: Map the ground
briefing: Before you read a single log line, map what is on disk. The on-call note says the host's fans spun up overnight, and nobody can name the process doing it.
Attackers rarely drop tools where `ls` shows them. Find the file that should not be there.

lesson.p: `find PATH TESTS` walks a directory tree and prints every path that passes all of its tests. Tests are joined with AND, left to right. `!` negates the next test; `-o` means OR.

flags: match the file name with shell wildcards. Quote it so the shell does not expand it first. -iname ignores case.
match the whole path. '*/.*' means: somewhere under a name that starts with a dot (a hidden directory or file).
bigger than / smaller than. Units round UP to whole units: c = bytes, k = KiB, M = MiB.
modified less than 24 hours ago / more than 7 full days ago
modified after an exact date and time; precise where -mtime counts whole days
any execute bit set / the owner's execute bit set
run CMD once with many paths; `{} \;` runs it once per path
separate paths with NUL bytes so names with spaces survive the pipe

lesson.note: `find` measures time from now. Inside this VM, now is 2026-03-14 02:40 UTC, the moment the pager fired. Run `date` to see it.
Size rounding catches people: a 1,100-byte file counts as 2 KiB, so it matches `-size +1k`. Use `c` (bytes) when the exact size matters.

examples.title: Walk a tree

stages.why: With no tests, find prints every path under the starting point, including directories and hidden names.
find prints in directory order, which is not alphabetical. Sorting makes the output stable and easy to compare.

examples.output:
training/drill
training/drill/.hidden
training/drill/.hidden/todo.txt
training/drill/empty.log
training/drill/notes.txt
training/drill/report final.txt

stages.why: Only regular files; directories have sizes too and would muddy the list.
More than 1 KiB after rounding up. web.log (1,145 bytes) rounds to 2 KiB and matches; audit.log (680 bytes) rounds to 1 KiB and does not.

examples.title: Count files older than a week

stages.why: The training files were written on 2026-03-01, about 13 days before now, so all of them are more than 7 full days old.
Count the lines find printed: one path per line, so this is the number of files.

examples.title: Why a plain pipe breaks on spaces

stages.why: Quoted, so find sees the wildcard instead of the shell expanding it in the current directory.
xargs splits its input on spaces and newlines, then runs echo once per piece (-n1). Watch the last file: report final.txt arrives as two separate names.
Stable order. Look for the two halves of report final.txt: `final.txt` sorts first, `training/drill/report` last.
End each path with a NUL byte instead of a newline. NUL is the one byte a Linux file name cannot contain.
-0 tells xargs to split on NUL only, so report final.txt stays one argument. `-exec echo {} +` would also be safe, because no pipe is involved.
Stable order: three files, three lines.

challenge.question: Somewhere in ~/arena is a regular file that has an execute bit set, sits under a hidden directory, and was modified in the last 24 hours. What is its path?
challenge.format: The path exactly as `find .` prints it when run from ~/arena, for example ./dir/file

hints: Three conditions, one find command: each condition is a test that must be true. Start it with `find .` from ~/arena so the path begins with ./
You need `-type f` (regular file), `-perm /111` (any execute bit), `-path '*/.*'` (under a hidden name), and `-mtime -1` (changed in the last 24 hours).

why: Attackers drop tooling in dot-directories under /tmp, /var/tmp, and /dev/shm because `ls` hides them and those directories are writable by everyone. `kworkerd` is named to blend in with the kernel's own kworker threads in `ps` output.

On a real RHEL host, an early triage sweep is `find /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm -xdev -type f -perm /111 -mtime -2`. `-mtime` counts whole 24-hour periods, so switch to `-newermt` with an exact timestamp once you know the incident window.
`-executable` asks whether you could run the file (it honours your user and ACLs). `-perm /111` reads the mode bits. As root the two can disagree, so be clear which question you are asking.
